frameworks.name: Three Affiliate Integration Modes
frameworks.definition: Alex Hormozi's ranked list of three ways to integrate an affiliate into your revenue: (1) give away your lead magnet free so they distribute it, (2) let them sell your lead magnet at 100% margin while you capture the customer relationship for upsell, (3) commission-based kickback on referred sales — ordered easiest to hardest to execute.

frameworks.name: Guarantee Formula
frameworks.definition: A structured template for any guarantee: 'If you don't X in Y time, we will Z.' The goal is to maximize net conversions (new sales minus refunds), not to offer the most extreme terms; the guaranteed element should address the customer's biggest fears.

frameworks.name: Launch-to-Integration Affiliate Activation
frameworks.definition: A two-phase model for converting a trial-referral affiliate into a fully activated partner: Phase 1 (Launch) — propose a big coordinated campaign to their customer base after the trial succeeds; Phase 2 (Integration) — embed the referral into the affiliate's standard sales process so it happens automatically without reminders.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that out-of-network insurance-based healthcare practices face a structural margin squeeze because insurance reimbursements decline annually while operational costs rise with inflation, and because the pool of patients with out-of-network benefits is shrinking as payers push everyone in-network. This squeeze produces zero-profit operations for practices that do not adapt.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: out-of-network insurance billing model
healthcare / chiropractic / PT practices
claims.mechanism: Reimbursements from payers decline annually while inflation raises costs, and the total addressable patient pool with out-of-network benefits contracts as employers and payers push patients to in-network providers.
bounded_by: In-network practices face the opposite dynamic — guaranteed patient volume but no pricing power; their constraint is operational efficiency, not margin.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for a business transitioning from insurance billing to cash-pay, the strategic path choice reduces to two fundamentally different operating models: cash-pay requires learning customer acquisition (ads, offers, selling), whereas in-network requires mastering operational efficiency because there is no pricing power in-network.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: healthcare / therapy / chiropractic practices choosing billing model
bounded_by: Does not apply to practices that have already built strong cash-pay acquisition skills or to those that have already optimized in-network operations.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that a local cash-pay healthcare practice advertising to new patients should run paid ads with a highly discounted front-end assessment offer (e.g., a $200 service for $19-20), collect a credit card on file at booking, and call new leads by phone within 60 seconds of inquiry. This sequence produces show rates of 70-80% on practitioner time compared to no-payment bookings.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: local brick-and-mortar healthcare / service practice
transitioning to cash-pay acquisition
inbound leads from paid ads
claims.mechanism: Requiring payment upfront creates a commitment device that filters non-serious prospects and reduces no-show rate; having a card on file also enables no-show fees and smooths the in-session upsell.
bounded_by: Does not apply to telehealth or remote services where no physical visit is required.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi advises selling at the point of greatest need, not the point of greatest satisfaction — specifically, in a healthcare assessment model the sale pitch should happen after the assessment reveals the problem but before treatment begins, because the prospect's desire for a solution peaks at that moment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: sell at point of greatest need, not point of greatest satisfaction
conditions: in-person assessment-based service businesses (healthcare, fitness, etc.)
claims.mechanism: Prospect motivation to purchase peaks when they have just learned the diagnosis of their problem and before they have received any relief; delivering value first reduces urgency and closes fewer deals.
bounded_by: Does not apply to self-serve digital products where there is no in-person assessment moment.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that education businesses structurally graduate their customers because the product's purpose is to teach — once learned, the customer has no reason to continue paying. The only durable continuity mechanism in education is always having a higher level of education to sell (analogous to undergrad → master's → PhD).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: live-event and mentorship education businesses where customers are taught a skill
claims.mechanism: Education that successfully delivers its promise eliminates the customer's need for that product; without a next-level offering the business must perpetually acquire new customers rather than retain existing ones.
bounded_by: Applies to done-for-you or taught-skill formats; less applicable to ongoing communities or curated information products where the value is access, not learning.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for an education business generating revenue from live events, the highest-leverage path to scaling revenue without operational risk is geographic expansion — running identical events in new regions — rather than inventing new revenue retention mechanisms, when the founder's stated goal is simply to make more money rather than to build a sellable asset.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: live-event education business with proven playbook
founder's goal is income, not company valuation or exit
bounded_by: If the founder wants to sell the company, revenue retention (recurring revenue) must be solved first because exit multiples depend on retention, not top-line revenue alone.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that a live-event education business with a $12,000 high-ticket offer consider creating a downsell membership at $3,000-$5,000 per year for graduates, because this recurring revenue allows the business to break even or even take a loss on the $12,000 event ticket — enabling the business to outspend competitors on acquisition.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: live-event education business with high-ticket mentorship offer
founder has alumni base that has completed the program
claims.mechanism: A $3,000-$5,000 annual membership that is mostly margin creates a recurring stack of revenue that funds aggressive CAC on the front-end event; competitors who must profit from the $12,000 event cannot outbid on acquisition.

numbers.axis: recurring membership price for education alumni

bounded_by: Requires the alumni to perceive ongoing value in continued access (network, vendors, events); does not work if the membership delivers nothing beyond the completed program.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that standard 20% referral kickback offers are ubiquitous and therefore ineffective at changing affiliate behavior — nearly no one actually refers business on a generic 20% commission. An affiliate offer must be compelling enough to change what the affiliate actually does in their business.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B affiliate/referral partner programs across service industries
claims.mechanism: When every competitor offers 20% kickbacks, the offer is undifferentiated and below the activation threshold that changes affiliate behavior; the offer must cross a threshold of value that causes the affiliate to alter their standard business process.
bounded_by: Commission-based structures can work if the commission is dramatically higher than the market standard, or if combined with making the referral frictionless.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's preferred affiliate integration model is letting affiliates sell the provider's lead magnet at 100% margin (the affiliate keeps all the money), in exchange for the customer introduction — because the lead magnet's hard cost is then the true customer acquisition cost, and the real money comes from upselling the introduced customer.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: businesses with a low-cost lead magnet (physical or digital) that affiliates can sell
claims.mechanism: Affiliates are maximally motivated when they keep 100% of revenue from what they sell; the provider's cost is only the hard cost of the lead magnet, and the introduced customer relationship becomes the channel for backend upsell at full margin.
bounded_by: Does not work when the lead magnet is the entire product (e.g. custom railings where a sample cannot be split from the full order); in that case, commission-based structures are necessary.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when changing a business model or offer, the expected value of the change must exceed the cost and risk of making the change. For a PE-backed roofing platform generating ~$300-$400 million in enterprise value, changing the core offer immediately after acquisition is high-risk relative to the guaranteed returns from operational centralization.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: post-acquisition integration context
business with stable EBITDA and proven model
PE platform with 8+ tuck-in acquisitions
claims.mechanism: Offer changes ripple through billing, advertising, and sales simultaneously; the probability-weighted upside must exceed the disruption risk. Centralization delivers near-certain EBITDA improvements without disrupting revenue.

numbers.axis: estimated enterprise value of roofing PE platform at time of discussion

bounded_by: When a business is unprofitable or declining, the cost of the status quo exceeds the cost of change and more aggressive pivots are warranted.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that centralizing a distributed roofing sales force into a remote sales team produces three simultaneous improvements: cost reduction (no on-road expenses), better talent access (remote hiring from a larger pool), and higher sales utilization (cutting low-performing reps). Together these can produce a ~25% EBITDA lift, which may be sufficient to meet exit valuation targets without any offer changes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: distributed field sales roofing business with local sales reps
PE platform context with near-term exit goals
claims.mechanism: Centralizing sales reduces fixed costs (vehicles, local offices), enables hiring from national rather than local talent pools at lower wages, and allows top performers to absorb the volume previously lost to low performers — all three levers reduce cost and increase revenue simultaneously.

numbers.axis: estimated EBITDA impact from sales centralization alone

anchors.region: EBITDA required to justify offer change risk

bounded_by: Specific to businesses where a significant portion of cost is field-based sales rep overhead; less applicable to businesses already using inside sales.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends structuring a home-services guarantee around customers' two primary fears — delivery on time and delivery on budget — rather than offering a full money-back guarantee. Refunding only the profit margin (e.g., 20%) rather than full revenue is often sufficient to shift buying behavior because the customer's goal is to get the roof, not the money back.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: home services businesses (roofing, construction, etc.) with high hard costs making full refunds unprofitable
claims.mechanism: Customers don't want a refund; they want the outcome delivered. A guarantee signals that the provider is aligned with the outcome. Any non-trivial financial skin-in-the-game crosses the threshold required to shift purchasing behavior; the marginal value of going from 20% to 100% refund is smaller than the marginal cost to the provider.
bounded_by: A guarantee that does not address the customer's specific fears (time and budget in home services) fails even if the dollar amount is large.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that the goal of a guarantee is to maximize net conversions (incremental new sales minus incremental refunds) — not to offer the most extreme terms. If a 10% refund and a 100% refund produce the same conversion lift, only 10% should be offered.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the highest-leverage move for an insurance sales organization with 29 agents is to teach agents to self-generate their own leads rather than feeding them leads from the founder's personal brand — because recruiting and training self-sufficient lead generators creates compounding nodes of production independent of founder effort.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: insurance or commission-based sales org with agents who depend on founder-supplied leads
founder has existing content/brand driving a minority of leads
claims.mechanism: Each self-generating agent becomes an independent revenue node; the founder's fixed effort gets multiplied across N agents rather than supplying leads to N agents serially. Lead-getter leverage (scenario 3) compounds exponentially versus lead-supply leverage (scenario 1) which scales linearly.
bounded_by: Only applies if agents can realistically be trained to self-generate; does not apply if the product requires company-level brand credibility to sell (e.g., enterprise SaaS).

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a demand-constrained insurance business (where agents can sell unlimited policies if they have leads) should prioritize recruiting and training more agents over acquiring more leads itself, because the business is supply-constrained in salespeople, not demand-constrained in willing buyers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: insurance / commission-based sales where regulatory capacity is not a constraint
founder has content brand generating organic leads
bounded_by: Does not apply to businesses where regulatory, physical capacity, or product constraints limit how many units can be sold regardless of sales effort.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi advises that a B2B mobile healthcare company (IV infusion, $6,000 per treatment) with 200 active physician affiliates averaging one referral each should prioritize fully activating the existing affiliate base before investing in B2C advertising, because each physician has access to thousands of patients and the business is getting only one referral per affiliate — indicating a systematic follow-up and integration failure rather than a market saturation problem.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: B2B affiliate-referral healthcare business
affiliates have high patient volume but low referral activation rate
existing B2B economics: $500 CAC, $6,000 average revenue per affiliate referral = 12:1 return
claims.mechanism: A one-referral-per-affiliate pattern indicates affiliates are in trial mode, not integrated mode; full activation of 200 affiliates who each refer at even 5% of their patient volume would produce far more revenue than starting a new B2C channel from zero.
bounded_by: Once the B2B affiliate channel is fully optimized and saturated in a given market, B2C advertising becomes the logical next investment.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that a prosumer software business (musicians' contract automation) with 40% month-12 retention should prioritize improving that single retention metric above all else — and use the education product's revenue as customer acquisition cost liquidation — because best-in-class annual retention for a consumer/prosumer product is 60%+ and closing that gap compounds automatically into revenue growth.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: prosumer SaaS targeting musicians or similar creative professionals
education product exists that can fund acquisition cost
claims.mechanism: Software with improving annual retention grows automatically because new cohorts add to the base without subtracting at the same rate; the education product liquidates CAC so the SaaS itself can be grown without needing to profit from acquisition.

numbers.axis: annual retention benchmark for consumer/prosumer SaaS

bounded_by: Does not apply to enterprise SaaS where retention dynamics differ and stickiness is contractual rather than value-driven.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a business founder considering a partner should only bring in a partner if the partner fills a genuine capability gap the founder cannot fill alone — because splitting equity for capabilities the founder already has or can hire for is economically suboptimal.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder evaluating whether to take on a business partner

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that in a cash-pay local service business, the front-end acquisition offer should be one to three tightly defined entry offers that convert profitably from ads, and the remaining 10-15 services are cross-sold and upsold after the customer walks in the door — rather than advertising all 15 services simultaneously.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: multi-service local brick-and-mortar business (healthcare, fitness, etc.) transitioning to paid acquisition
bounded_by: Does not apply to high-intent inbound search (SEO) businesses where users self-select service; applies primarily to paid advertising where offer specificity drives conversion.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that in a SaaS marketplace business, the best marketplaces shift to a flat subscription model (like Shopify at $29/month) rather than revenue-share, because charging a percentage of zero revenue from the majority of users produces less total revenue than a small flat fee that prosumer users pay on the hope of future income.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: two-sided marketplace or platform where the majority of supply-side users generate zero or near-zero revenue
prosumer audience (aspiring professionals)
claims.mechanism: Users pay a flat subscription for access and the optionality of future income even when they currently earn nothing; revenue-share on zero produces zero for the platform. The prosumer motivation is hope of future earnings, which justifies a monthly fee.
bounded_by: Requires enough perceived future upside that users will pay before earning; does not work for commodity tools with no aspiration dimension.

examples.text: A restoration roofing company used a single top salesman whose entire job was visiting other tradesmen (electricians, plumbers, etc.) with coffee and donuts, reminding them that the restoration company existed, and activating their referrals — paying each tradesman $1,000 per referral and the salesman $500 per activation. This kept 200+ affiliate relationships continuously warm without any formal system. Alex Hormozi cited this as the model for how a dedicated affiliate manager generates consistent referral volume.

Henry, a Spanish-language real-estate education entrepreneur in Miami, runs two large events per year of 600 people each, converts 20% to a $12,000 mentorship, then loses 100% of both groups forever — the 80% who didn't buy see nothing else to purchase and the 20% who bought complete the mentorship and graduate. Alex Hormozi used this to illustrate that education products structurally graduate their customers and that continuity requires building a 'next level' offering.

James, who sells custom stair railings nationwide via SEO, attracted his two largest customers ($50,000 and $60,000 projects) organically through architects who had specified his product in their plans. Alex Hormozi used this to illustrate that B2B architect affiliates are worth pursuing but require a compelling incentive beyond a standard 20% kickback — in James's case, the inability to offer a partial product sample forced a commission-based structure rather than the preferred lead-magnet-resale model.

A hypothetical marker business: if a marker costs 50 cents to produce and an affiliate can sell it for $5 and keep 100%, the provider acquires a buyer relationship at 50 cents. If 1 in 2 marker buyers then purchase the other three colors at $5 each, the effective CAC through the affiliate is $1 (two deliveries at 50 cents each) while the revenue per converted customer is $20. Alex Hormozi used this to illustrate why the lead-magnet-at-100%-margin model is his preferred affiliate structure.

Cody, the founder and CEO of a roofing company that did $140 million in revenue (retail only, no storm-chasing), was 30 days post-acquisition by a PE firm that had also acquired seven other roofing companies. He asked for an irresistible offer to roll out across all eight brands. Alex Hormozi argued against immediately changing the offer — estimating the aggregate enterprise value at $300-400 million — and instead recommended centralizing all sales to remote/virtual first, as that change was already part of the acquisition deal and would deliver 25%+ EBITDA improvement with far lower execution risk.

Mohamed, founder of El Fan (a creator tools platform), had 40,000 creators signed up but only 1,000 generating any revenue, and was running a music label, creator agency, and platform simultaneously. Alex Hormozi described this as the cardinal sin of chasing multiple rabbits, and argued that winning in SaaS requires going all-in because competitors are typically well-funded and also very smart — split attention cannot compete with focused competitors.

practices.text: When building an affiliate referral program for a home-services or professional services business, design the offer so the affiliate would be stupid to say no — not a generic 20% kickback, but something that changes what they actually do in their business (e.g., a product they can sell at 100% margin, or a major commission that materially improves their revenue).

For a physician affiliate referral business, close the patient feedback loop with the referring physician immediately after the patient's visit: report on the patient's experience (without violating privacy), then ask 'Which patients did you see this week who would be a good fit?' rather than 'Do you have any referrals?' — the specific framing anchors the conversation to specific patients rather than an open-ended ask.

When transitioning a multi-avatar service business to paid acquisition, identify the one to three offers that convert most profitably as the front-door, then cross-sell and upsell the full menu after the customer is inside. Do not advertise all services simultaneously.
Never count the other person's money in an affiliate deal. Focus only on whether the deal economics work for you; what the affiliate earns is irrelevant as long as your unit economics are positive.

When introducing an affiliate or referral partner to your business, treat the first referral as a trial: the first patient or customer must be given a 'beautifully choreographed experience' because the affiliate is evaluating whether to trust you with their own reputation before committing to ongoing referrals.

For an insurance or commission-based sales organization that wants to scale, alternate content call-to-actions between end customers and prospective agents — the same educational content attracts both audiences, and dual CTAs allow double-dipping without changing the content strategy.
